note: What each project did and why, in two or three sentences, from the project's own SFMTA page (cached under data/sfmta-pages/, read 2026-09-24). Words in quotation marks are the page's own. A project whose page text could not be read has no entry, and the card shows none. Bryan, 2026-09-24: "Write down a 2-3 sentence summary based on the MTA project page that tries to capture what and why ... include direct quotes wherever appropriate."

summaries.1128: A north-south route through the Sunset to Golden Gate Park and Stern Grove, meant to be "a more pleasant north-south route for people walking and biking". It added "a bike lane in the uphill directions, speed cushions" and turned some angled parking to parallel. The SFMTA Board approved it on June 4, 2019.
summaries.653: 7th and 8th Streets are a one-way couplet in SoMa whose design, with freeway ramps and the 19-Polk, "presents the potential for crashes between people walking, bicycling, taking transit and driving." The project brought quick-build safety changes to what the page calls "important bicycle network links" to Mission Bay and Caltrain.
summaries.27619: Shotwell Street, from 14th Street to Cesar Chavez, is "an important north-south connection through the Mission neighborhood." It began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street in June 2020 and the SFMTA Board affirmed it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022.
summaries.27612: Clay Street from Arguello Boulevard to Steiner Street in Pacific Heights began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street in 2021. The SFMTA Board approved it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022, with targets of "Vehicle speeds at or below 15 mph" and "Vehicle volumes less than 1,000 per day".
summaries.24645: A joint SFMTA and Recreation and Park program that made permanent "the 3-mile stretch of car-free streets in the park from Lincoln Way to Kezar Drive, including JFK Drive." Other parts include "a vastly improved free Park Shuttle program" and "bringing bikeshare and micromobility services to the park". The Board of Supervisors approved it on April 26, 2022.
summaries.21264: A 2019 quick-build "protected two-way bikeway" on Terry Francois Boulevard, opened in time for the Chase Center. The page says it gives people on bikes "an attractive alternative to the busy Third Street corridor" and will become part of the San Francisco Bay Trail.
summaries.15731: Valencia Street "has been a key Mission District corridor in the bikeway network for more than 25 years." The project rebuilt its bikeway to improve "safety and comfort" on a street the page calls one of the country's biggest collections of independent businesses.
summaries.1092: The goal was "a safe and pleasant north-south route for people walking and biking in the Inner Richmond." The project used "speed humps, painted markings, stop signs, and other measures" on 8th Avenue.
summaries.27620: Sanchez Street through Noe Valley is a Slow Street connecting destinations like the Upper Noe Recreation Center. It began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street in June 2020 and the SFMTA Board affirmed it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022.
summaries.1122: SFMTA's summary: "Improving safety on Vicente Street". The project page text beyond that could not be read.
summaries.381: Folsom and Howard are three- and four-lane one-way arterials "designed for trucks and cars serving the manufacturing and warehousing industry". With SoMa's growth in housing and jobs, the page says "Walkways and bikeways are currently inadequate", and the project rebuilds both streets for walking, biking and transit.
summaries.1032: A Recreation and Park project, with SFMTA and Public Works, on Twin Peaks Boulevard. The SFMTA and RPD "implemented the Twin Peaks Pilot Promenade" in July 2016, and the pilot configuration "was made permanent in June 2020".
summaries.1146: The project "improves safety along the corridor for those who walk, bike, and drive" on 5th Street. Its first phase, the 5th Street Quick Build completed in 2020, "installed time and cost efficient, short-term upgrades"; a permanent project follows.
summaries.24767: Lake Street from 28th Avenue to Arguello Boulevard is "an important east-west connection through the Richmond neighborhood." It began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street in April 2020 and the SFMTA Board affirmed it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022.
summaries.853: Masonic Avenue between Geary and Fell was on the city's Vision Zero High Injury Network. The project rebuilt it with "wider sidewalks, a new median, new paving, landscaping, raised bikeways, better lighting and upgraded sewer infrastructure."
summaries.27614: Hearst Avenue from Ridgewood Avenue to Baden Street in Sunnyside began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street in 2021. The SFMTA Board approved it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022.
summaries.1204: 2nd Street from Market to King, which the East SoMa Area Plan named "a primary pedestrian, bicycle and transit thoroughfare". The project aimed at "transforming 2nd Street into a pleasant multi-modal corridor".
summaries.807: SFMTA, SFPUC and Public Works rebuilt the Wiggle with stormwater management and bike and pedestrian safety changes. The goal: "a route that is comfortable and safe for all who walk, bike, and live along the Wiggle".
summaries.27618: Somerset Street from Silver Avenue to Woolsey Street in the Portola began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street in 2021. The SFMTA Board approved it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022.
summaries.27615: Lyon Street from Turk Street to Haight Street began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street. The SFMTA Board approved it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022.
summaries.27602: 12th Avenue from Lincoln Way to Lawton Street in the Inner Sunset began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street in 2021. The SFMTA Board approved it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022.
summaries.23813: Part of the Vision Zero Quick-Build Program, the project "assessed the feasibility of protected bikeways and implemented improvements on Battery and Sansome streets" between Market and Vallejo. It extends the earlier Sansome Battery Connections work to give a better bike connection to and from the Financial District.
summaries.27467: The project "adds a two-way protected bikeway on the east side of Frida Kahlo Way / south side of Judson Avenue". Its purpose is to strengthen walking and biking connections between Sunnyside, Ingleside, the Ocean Avenue corridor and City College.
summaries.1305: The "Bernal Cut" of San Jose Avenue "hosts freeway-like conditions on a city street", partly fed by a two-lane I-280 off-ramp. The pilot narrowed it to slow vehicles and "increase safety and comfort for all road users".
summaries.27608: Arlington Street from Roanoke Street to Randall Street in Glen Park began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street in 2021. The SFMTA Board approved it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022.
summaries.1202: Polk Street carries the 19 Polk and is "a preferred north-south bicycle route due to its flatter terrain." The streetscape project redesigned it to improve "safety for all road users on Polk Street".
summaries.27603: 23rd Avenue from Lake Street to Cabrillo Street in the Richmond began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street in 2021. The SFMTA Board approved it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022.
summaries.22078: Evans Avenue between Cesar Chavez and 3rd streets is on the city's Vision Zero High Injury Network, with "81 crashes involving a vehicle and another vehicle, bicyclist or pedestrian" from 2015 to 2020. The quick-build's "main goal is to improve traffic safety conditions and comfort for all who travel along Evans Avenue", using "adjustable, quick-to-construct, and reversible roadway treatments". Construction was completed in summer 2022.
summaries.21903: Quick-build changes along the waterfront at Pier 35, the Ferry Terminal and the Rincon restaurant zone, completed in early 2021. They included "the corridor's first segment of a two-way protected bikeway adjacent to the promenade (between Folsom and Mission streets)".
summaries.851: Turk Street between Market and Gough was chosen "based on its inclusion on the Vision Zero High Injury Network", the 13 percent of streets with 75 percent of injuries and deaths. The project added safety changes along a dense corridor of families, seniors, workers and students.
summaries.1102: Townsend Street has "one of the richest mixes of travel modes of any street in San Francisco", centered on the Caltrain station at 4th and Townsend. The project redesigned it for the thousands of people an hour who reach the station by bike, on foot, by rail and by bus.
summaries.45035: Winston Drive from Lake Merced Boulevard to Buckingham Way gets "a separated bikeway, new transit boarding islands, pedestrian safety improvements, and parking modifications." The work is coordinated with a Public Works repaving project.
summaries.28173: Lapu-Lapu, Rizal, Tandang Sora, Bonifacio and Mabini streets between Folsom and Harrison in SoMa began as COVID-19 Response Slow Streets in 2021. The SFMTA Board approved them as permanent Slow Streets on May 16, 2023.
summaries.1134: SFMTA's summary: "Bringing safety improvements for all road users on Brannan Street". The rest of the project page could not be read.
summaries.17131: The "Alemany Maze" interchange "has long acted as a barrier between the adjacent communities of the Portola, Bernal Heights, Silver Terrace, and the Bayview." The project added "new protected bike lanes on Alemany Boulevard between Putnam Street/I-280 N off-ramp and Bayshore Boulevard" and "a buffered bike lane southbound on San Bruno Avenue from Alemany Boulevard to Silver Avenue", unveiled in March 2021. The page notes "No changes to parking will be made".
summaries.879: The 9 San Bruno "serves many of San Francisco's working-class neighborhoods" from Visitacion Valley to the Financial District. Since 2009 the SFMTA has added "dedicated red transit lanes" and safety features for people walking along its route.
summaries.16577: Indiana Street (Bicycle Route 7) "had no bike lanes between 23rd Street to Cesar Chavez" because of one-way traffic to the I-280 on-ramp. The goal was "a safe and comfortable north-south bike route connection in the Dogpatch Neighborhood."
summaries.1075: "The SFMTA is proposing to upgrade Bryant Street between Division and 17th Streets in coordination with repaving with new bike facilities and streamlined Muni stops."
summaries.219: On 17th Street between Church and Sanchez, "People on bicycles are being injured in falls" on the streetcar tracks and poor pavement. Past fixes had not stopped the crashes, and "people with disabilities are having a difficult time crossing the street."
summaries.21852: An emergency COVID-19 response: "a parking protected bikeway on Fell Street between Baker Street and Shrader Street to provide relief to crowding and support social distancing on the Panhandle Path."
summaries.20650: Quick-build changes on community-chosen Bayview streets, aimed at "improving pedestrian visibility and comfort at crossings and reducing vehicle speeds." Streets on the Vision Zero High Injury Network, such as Williams Avenue, came first.
summaries.27609: Cabrillo Street from 45th Avenue to 23rd Avenue in the Richmond began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street. The SFMTA Board approved it as a permanent Slow Street on December 6, 2022.
summaries.24778: Golden Gate Avenue is a Slow Street through North of the Panhandle, "an important connection ... to parks, schools, and the University of San Francisco." It began as a COVID-19 Response Slow Street in June 2020 and the SFMTA Board affirmed it on December 6, 2022.
summaries.28896: Beach Street from The Embarcadero to Polk Street in Fisherman's Wharf. The project covers "pedestrian and bicycle safety improvements, curb management changes and traffic signal retiming."
summaries.1012: Division and 13th Streets are "a key east-west corridor for people biking" to Caltrain, the Mission and South Beach. "In a five year period alone, there were 106 collisions along the Division/13th Street corridor, including two traffic deaths."
summaries.1267: A traffic calming project "initiated by area residents to help reduce the negative impacts of motor vehicle traffic while improving safety and access for people walking and biking." The measures on local streets came from resident input and traffic surveys.
summaries.2082: Public Works repaved Upper Clipper Street, and SFMTA used the repaving to answer "community requests for traffic calming." The chosen design "keep[s] the center turn lane and retain[s] all existing parking."
summaries.28710: 3rd Street from the Bay Trail to Townsend Street connects Mission Bay, SoMa and Oracle Park. The project aims to "improve bike network connectivity" and deliver "transportation safety and comfort on the project corridor for all users".
summaries.17912: The project gave people walking and biking between the Embarcadero and the Financial District "an alternative route parallel to the traffic-heavy Embarcadero corridor", with new bike lanes on Sansome and Battery. It was fully completed in December 2019.
summaries.24472: Lake Merced Boulevard from Skyline to John Muir Drive got "roadway reallocation and lane narrowing". Its two goals: traffic calming "to reduce collisions" and "safe pedestrian and bicycle connections to or along Lake Merced Boulevard".
summaries.27583: The Upper Great Highway, the two miles between Lincoln Way and Sloat Boulevard, became a car-free promenade during the COVID-19 pandemic. The page says it has provided outdoor space "for families, people on bicycles and in wheelchairs".
summaries.20166: On Howard Street between 3rd Street and the Embarcadero the project would "upgrade the existing bike lane to a parking-protected bike lane", add a bike signal at 3rd Street and transit boarding islands, and reduce vehicle lanes. The page says the work "is complete."
summaries.24302: Howard Street between 4th Street and The Embarcadero "serves as a well-traveled east-west bike route" past Moscone Center and the Transbay Terminal. The project rebuilds the streetscape along that stretch.
summaries.26713: A quick-build on 17th Street in Potrero Hill, "unanimously approved at the March 5th SFMTA Board of Directors meeting". Construction is complete, and SFMTA will evaluate it "within 24 months of implementation."
summaries.20169: "a temporary improvement to traffic safety" on Folsom Street, "fully complete" at the end of 2021. The permanent redesign comes later under the Folsom-Howard Streetscape Project.
summaries.24436: "Every street in the Tenderloin is on the city's Vision Zero High Injury Network." The quick-build builds off the COVID-19 response work on Jones Street, including the 2020 physical distancing lanes from O'Farrell Street to Golden Gate Avenue, with "adjustable and reversible traffic safety improvements". The page reports "Construction is complete on Jones Street!"
summaries.21263: Part of the Tenderloin quick-builds that "Stemmed from the community's demand for increased investment" in traffic safety. It installed "quick and reversible traffic safety improvements" to "improve comfort and safety for those walking and biking along Golden Gate Avenue."
